_meta.notes: Comprehensive index for Bhutan covering early Bon religion, Guru Rinpoche (Padmasambhava) and Buddhism, Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal unification (1616), Dzong fortress system, British influence, Wangchuck monarchy (1907), modernisation under third and fourth kings, Gross National Happiness, democratic transition 2008, and Lhotshampa refugee crisis.

country_profile.currency: Bhutanese ngultrum (BTN) / Indian rupee (INR, pegged and accepted)

religion.note: Buddhism is state religion; Drukpa Kagyu school and Nyingma school; Hinduism mainly among southern Lhotshampa (Nepali-origin)

ethnic_groups.name: Ngalop
ethnic_groups.notes: Western/northern Bhutan; Tibeto-Burman; Dzongkha-speaking; politically dominant; Drukpa Kagyu Buddhist; built dzong fortress culture

ethnic_groups.name: Sharchop (Tshangla)
ethnic_groups.notes: Eastern Bhutan; believed to be earliest inhabitants; Tibeto-Burman; Tshangla language; Nyingma Buddhist tradition

ethnic_groups.name: Lhotshampa (Nepali-origin)
ethnic_groups.notes: Southern Bhutan; Indo-Aryan; Nepali-speaking; Hindu; migrated 19th-20th century; ~100,000 expelled/fled in 1990s 'One Nation One People' policy; resettled in US, Canada, Australia

ethnic_groups.name: Other (Kheng, Bumthap, Mangde, Layap, Brokpa)
ethnic_groups.notes: Central Bhutanese groups; Layap semi-nomadic yak herders in high altitudes; Brokpa in Merak-Sakteng; diverse small groups

independence.notes: Treaty of Punakha 1910 with Britain (external affairs guidance); revised 1949 with India; sovereign since 2007 friendship treaty revision

country_profile.notes_unique: Only carbon-negative country; Gross National Happiness (GNH) over GDP; no traffic lights in capital; last country to introduce television (1999); prohibited tobacco sales

current_leader.name: Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck
current_leader.title: King (Druk Gyalpo)
current_leader.notes: Fifth King; 'People's King'; Oxford-educated; presided over democratic transition; popular; married Queen Jetsun Pema 2011

prime_minister.name: Tshering Tobgay
prime_minister.title: Prime Minister
prime_minister.notes: PDP; second term (previously 2013-2018); Gelephu Mindfulness City project

former_kings.name: Ugyen Wangchuck
former_kings.notes: First King; unified Bhutan; Penlop of Trongsa; established hereditary monarchy

former_kings.name: Jigme Wangchuck
former_kings.notes: Second King; isolationist; consolidated royal authority

former_kings.name: Jigme Dorji Wangchuck
former_kings.notes: Third King; 'Father of Modern Bhutan'; abolished serfdom; joined UN 1971; modernisation

former_kings.name: Jigme Singye Wangchuck
former_kings.notes: Fourth King; invented Gross National Happiness concept; voluntarily abdicated in favour of son; drafted constitution for democracy

910.name: Early Bhutan and Buddhist Arrival
910.description: The prehistoric settlement of the eastern Himalayan valleys, early stone-tool cultures, and the arrival of Buddhism with Padmasambhava (Guru Rinpoche) in the 8th century.

sub_clusters.name: Prehistoric and Early Settlement
sub_clusters.description: The earliest human habitation in Bhutan's valleys, megalithic stone structures, and the region's isolation in the eastern Himalayas with sparse historical records before Buddhist missionaries.

sub_clusters.name: Padmasambhava and Buddhist Foundation
sub_clusters.description: The legendary visit of Guru Padmasambhava (Guru Rinpoche) who is credited with introducing Vajrayana Buddhism to Bhutan, the founding of sacred sites including Taktsang (Tiger's Nest), and the establishment of Buddhism as the dominant faith.
key_events: Guru Padmasambhava visits Bhutan and meditates at the Tiger's Nest cliff site (c. 747 AD)

920.name: Medieval Bhutan and Buddhist Lineages
920.description: The establishment of Buddhist monastic lineages, the arrival of Tibetan lamas fleeing political turmoil, the Drukpa Kagyu school's rise to prominence, and the fragmented rule of local chieftains.

sub_clusters.name: Tibetan Buddhist Missionaries
sub_clusters.description: Waves of Tibetan Buddhist missionaries establishing monasteries, the Nyingma, Kagyu, and other schools competing for influence, and the gradual Tibetanization of Bhutanese culture and religion.

sub_clusters.name: Drukpa Kagyu Ascendancy
sub_clusters.description: The Drukpa Kagyu lineage's establishment in Bhutan by Phajo Drugom Zhigpo, competition with other Buddhist schools, the construction of early dzongs (fortresses), and the decentralized rule of competing religious lords.
key_events: Phajo Drugom Zhigpo brings the Drukpa Kagyu lineage to Bhutan from Tibet (c. 1222)

920.name: Zhabdrung Unification
920.description: Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal's flight from Tibet and his remarkable unification of Bhutan, the establishment of the dual system of government, the construction of great dzongs, and the repulsion of Tibetan invasions.

sub_clusters.name: Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal
sub_clusters.description: The Tibetan lama Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal's unification of Bhutan, his creation of the unique dual system (religious and secular leaders), the codification of Driglam Namzha (national etiquette), and the construction of magnificent dzong fortresses.
key_events: Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal arrives in Bhutan and begins unifying the country (1616)
Bhutan repulses three major Tibetan-Mongol invasions under the Zhabdrung's leadership (1634–1649)

sub_clusters.name: Dzong Fortress System
sub_clusters.description: The construction of the great dzongs — Simtokha, Punakha, Trongsa, and others — as combined administrative, monastic, and military centers that define Bhutan's unique architectural heritage.

930.name: Era of Desis and Civil Conflicts
930.description: The long period after the Zhabdrung's death when his passing was concealed, the rule of successive Druk Desis, internal civil wars between eastern and western factions, and conflicts with Tibet and the British.

sub_clusters.name: Concealment of Zhabdrung's Death and Desi Rule
sub_clusters.description: The Zhabdrung's death concealed for 54 years to maintain stability, the succession of Druk Desis (temporal rulers), the war with Tibet and the Cooch Behar conflicts, and growing internal factionalism.

sub_clusters.name: Internal Wars and British Encounters
sub_clusters.description: Escalating civil wars between the penlops (governors) of Paro and Trongsa, the British East India Company's involvement, the Duar War of 1864–65, and the Treaty of Sinchula ceding southern Bhutan.
key_events: Duar War — Bhutan loses the Duars (southern plains) to British India via the Treaty of Sinchula (1865)

940.name: Wangchuck Monarchy Founding
940.description: Ugyen Wangchuck's consolidation of power, the establishment of the hereditary Wangchuck monarchy ending centuries of civil strife, the Treaty of Punakha with Britain, and Bhutan's splendid isolation.

sub_clusters.name: Ugyen Wangchuck Unification
sub_clusters.description: Penlop Ugyen Wangchuck's defeat of his rivals, his diplomatic role in the Younghusband Expedition to Tibet, and his election as the first hereditary King (Druk Gyalpo) of Bhutan.
key_events: Ugyen Wangchuck elected first King of Bhutan by an assembly of monks, officials, and people (1907)
Treaty of Punakha — Bhutan accepts British guidance in foreign affairs in exchange for autonomy (1910)

sub_clusters.name: Second King and Early Reforms
sub_clusters.description: King Jigme Wangchuck's cautious consolidation, Bhutan's complete isolation during the colonial period, the abolition of serfdom, and the transition from British to Indian suzerainty after Indian independence.

940.name: Third King and Modernization
940.description: King Jigme Dorji Wangchuck's transformation of Bhutan from a medieval hermit kingdom into a modern state, the first roads, schools, hospitals, and Bhutan's admission to the United Nations.

sub_clusters.name: Opening of Bhutan
sub_clusters.description: The Third King's abolition of slavery, land reform, the National Assembly, the first modern schools and hospitals, the first motorable road, and Bhutan's entry into the United Nations.
key_events: Bhutan joins the United Nations, formally entering the international community (1971)

950.name: Fourth King and Gross National Happiness
950.description: King Jigme Singye Wangchuck's revolutionary Gross National Happiness philosophy, careful development preserving culture and environment, the southern Bhutan crisis, and the voluntary transition to democracy.

sub_clusters.name: Gross National Happiness Philosophy
sub_clusters.description: The Fourth King's articulation of Gross National Happiness (GNH) as Bhutan's development philosophy, environmental conservation mandating 60% forest cover, cultural preservation policies, and carefully managed tourism.
key_events: King Jigme Singye Wangchuck declares 'Gross National Happiness is more important than Gross National Product' (1972)

sub_clusters.name: Southern Bhutan Crisis
sub_clusters.description: The Driglam Namzha cultural policy, the Lhotshampa (ethnic Nepali) crisis, the expulsion of approximately 100,000 Lhotshampa from southern Bhutan, and the refugee camps in Nepal.

sub_clusters.name: Democratic Transition
sub_clusters.description: The King's unprecedented voluntary devolution of absolute power, the drafting of the constitution, mock elections to prepare citizens for democracy, and the first democratic elections.
key_events: King Jigme Singye Wangchuck abdicates in favor of his son and Bhutan holds its first democratic elections (2008)

960.name: Constitutional Monarchy and Modern Bhutan
960.description: Bhutan's young democracy under the Fifth King, Gross National Happiness in practice, the carbon-negative economy, the digital Drukyul initiative, and the balance between tradition and modernization.

sub_clusters.name: Fifth King and Democratic Consolidation
sub_clusters.description: King Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck's popular reign, the consolidation of parliamentary democracy, Bhutan's position as the world's only carbon-negative country, and the royal wedding inspiring national pride.
key_events: Bhutan declares itself carbon-negative, with forests absorbing more CO₂ than the nation emits

sub_clusters.name: Gelephu Mindfulness City and Future Challenges
sub_clusters.description: The ambitious Gelephu Mindfulness City special administrative region, youth unemployment and emigration challenges, climate change threats to glacial watersheds, and Bhutan's unique development model.

unassigned_events.note: Events not yet assigned to a thematic cluster
